# The Time Machine

*Interest, Compounding and Discounting: Why a Euro Today Is Not a Euro Tomorrow*

## Opening: The \$700 Million Contract

::: {.details}
#### Story: The \$700 Million Contract
In December 2023, the baseball star Shohei Ohtani signed a ten-year contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers worth US\$700 million, at the time the largest contract in the history of professional sport. The headlines wrote themselves. Then the details emerged. During the ten playing seasons from 2024 to 2033, Ohtani receives only US\$2 million a year. The other US\$68 million of each year's salary is deferred: it is paid out, without interest, in ten instalments from 2034 to 2043, long after the contract's last pitch.

Ohtani and the Dodgers both accepted the deal. Ohtani gets exactly US\$700 million, to the cent. The Dodgers pay exactly US\$700 million, to the cent. And yet the league's own luxury-tax rules (a levy on teams whose payroll exceeds a threshold) value the contract at roughly US\$46 million a year, about US\$460 million in total, and that is still not what the contract was worth on the day it was signed.

Where did US\$240 million go?
:::

Nobody stole it. The money disappeared into time. A dollar paid in 2043 is not the same thing as a dollar paid in 2024, and every financial professional involved in the deal knew it. The Dodgers only have to set aside the present value of each deferred payment, money that then earns interest until it is paid out; Ohtani, who reportedly proposed the deferral himself, accepted later money to give the team room to afford other star players. The nominal sum, US\$700 million, is the least informative number in the whole story.

This idea runs through the entire course. Every decision in this book compares money that arrives at different points in time: a machine paid for today against savings over the next ten years, a loan received today against repayments spread over twenty, a bond bought today against coupons that run until maturity. Net present value, internal rate of return, annuity loans, bond prices and the after-tax discount rate are all built from the same operation, moving a payment along a timeline. If you master that operation in this chapter, the rest of the book is applications. If you do not, every later formula will feel like magic.

The guiding question of this chapter is simple and slightly provocative: *Why would anyone accept less than a euro today in exchange for a euro tomorrow?* We first build the economic intuition (why money has a price at all), then the formal toolkit (simple and compound interest, sub-annual compounding, discounting and real returns), and finally apply it to Ohtani's contract and to an everyday savings decision.

## Theory: The Price of Time

### Why Money Has a Time Value

The **time value of money** (dt. *Zeitwert des Geldes*) is the principle that a sum of money available today is worth more than the same sum available later. Interest is the price that makes the two comparable. Three forces drive that price, and every interest rate you will ever see is a mixture of them.

**Opportunity cost and time preference.** Money you hold today can be put to work today: deposited, lent or invested in a machine. Waiting for the same amount means giving up whatever that money could have earned in the meantime. That forgone return is the opportunity cost of waiting. Behind it sits a basic human trait: people prefer consumption now to consumption later and must be paid to postpone it. Economists call this *time preference*, and the classic treatment of interest as the meeting point of impatience and investment opportunity goes back to Irving Fisher (Fisher, 1930).

::: {.flip-card}
#### Opportunity Cost
The return on the best alternative you give up when you choose one use of money over another. In finance, the opportunity cost of receiving money later is the interest you could have earned on it in the meantime. That forgone interest is why a later payment must be larger than an earlier one to be equally attractive.
:::

**Inflation.** Even a perfectly patient investor faces a second problem: prices rise. If a basket of groceries costs €100 today and €103 next year, €100 received next year buys less than €100 today. A lender who wants to get back the same *purchasing power* must ask for compensation for expected inflation on top of the pure price of time.

**Risk.** Finally, a promise to pay is only as good as the person making it. A borrower may default, pay late or pay less. Lenders demand a **risk premium** for carrying that danger, and the premium grows with the borrower's credit risk and with the length of the commitment. This is why a start-up pays more for a loan than a large utility, and why both pay more than the German federal government.

The three drivers stack. Start with the *real risk-free rate*, the pure price of time for a perfectly safe borrower in a world without inflation. Add expected inflation and you get a nominal risk-free rate, for which the yields of top-rated government bonds such as German Bunds are the usual market proxy (a bond's *yield* is the annual return an investor earns by buying it at today's market price; Chapter 3 treats it in detail). Add a premium for default risk, and you arrive at the rate a particular borrower actually pays. The layers add up only approximately; the Fisher equation in the Method section shows the exact link between nominal rate and inflation. Central banks influence this structure at its short end: the European Central Bank sets *nominal* short-term policy rates, for example its deposit facility rate, the rate banks earn when they park money with the central bank overnight. Market rates for longer maturities and riskier borrowers build on top of them.

The interest stack below makes the layers visible. Hover over each layer and ask yourself which one would grow if inflation expectations rose, and which one would grow if the borrower were a cash-strapped start-up rather than the federal government.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Risk-Free Rate
The interest rate on a borrower who will pay with certainty. In theory it is the pure price of time; in practice it is approximated by the yield on top-rated government bonds of the same maturity. It is quoted in nominal terms, so it already contains expected inflation unless it is explicitly stated as a real rate.
:::

### Nominal and Real Interest

The rate printed on a bank statement is a **nominal interest rate** (dt. *Nominalzins*): it tells you how many more *euros* you will have. What you actually care about is how many more *goods* you will be able to buy. That is the **real interest rate** (dt. *Realzins*): the growth of purchasing power after inflation.

The difference is not academic. In October 2022, annual inflation in the euro area reached 10.6%, the highest rate since the series began in 1997. Picture a saver whose savings account paid 0.5% that year. Her balance grew by 0.5%; the prices of what she buys grew by more than 10%. In euros she became slightly richer. In bread, rent and energy she became roughly 9% poorer. The nominal rate said "gain"; the real rate said "loss".

The rough rule is intuitive: the real rate is approximately the nominal rate minus inflation. The Method section gives the exact form and shows when the rough rule breaks down.

::: {.drag-exercise}
The rate on your bank statement measures growth in *euros* and is called the *nominal* rate, while the growth of what those euros can buy is measured by the *real* rate.
:::

::: {.details}
#### Deep Dive: Two Different Meanings of "Nominal"
The word *nominal* carries two different contrasts in finance, and textbooks rarely warn you. **Nominal vs. real** is about inflation: a nominal rate measures growth in money, a real rate measures growth in purchasing power. **Nominal vs. effective** is about compounding: a nominal annual rate of 6% "paid monthly" is a quoted headline figure, while the effective annual rate (6.17% in this case, see the Method section) is what you actually earn over a year once monthly interest earns interest of its own. German banking language mirrors this second contrast with *Nominalzins* vs. *Effektivzins*. The formula collection uses the same symbol $i_{nom}$ in both contexts, so always check which contrast a task is about. A rate can be nominal in both senses at once: a savings offer of "3% p.a., paid monthly" is neither inflation-adjusted nor compounding-adjusted.
:::

::: {.quick-check}
Your savings account pays 2% per year, and inflation over the same year is 3%. What happens to your savings?

- Nothing changes, because you still receive positive interest.
- **You have more euros, but they buy less than your original balance did.**
- You have fewer euros at the end of the year than at the start.
:::

## Method: Moving Money Through Time

All tools in this chapter work on a single picture: a **timeline**. Today is $t = 0$; $t = 1$ is the end of the first period, $t = 2$ the end of the second, and so on. Unless a task says otherwise, a period is one year and a payment "in year $t$" arrives at the *end* of that year. Money moves along the line in two directions. **Compounding** (dt. *Aufzinsen*) moves a value forward, from left to right; **discounting** (dt. *Abzinsen*) moves it backward, from right to left.

| $t$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | … | $n$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Point in time | today | end of year 1 | end of year 2 | … | end of year $n$ |
| Value | $PV$ | | | | $FV$ |
| Compounding | → | → | → | → | |
| Discounting | | ← | ← | ← | ← |

Here $PV$ is the **present value** (dt. *Barwert*), the value at $t = 0$, and $FV$ is the **future value** (dt. *Endwert*), the value at $t = n$. The interest rate per period is $i$, written as a decimal (5% = 0.05), and $n$ is the number of periods.

### Simple Interest

Under **simple interest** (dt. *einfache Verzinsung*), interest is paid only on the original amount, never on interest already earned. Each period adds the same fixed amount $PV \cdot i$:

$$FV = PV \cdot (1 + n \cdot i)$$ {#eq-simple}

**Example:** €1,000 at 10% simple interest for three years earns €100 each year:

$$FV = 1{,}000 \cdot (1 + 3 \cdot 0.10) = 1{,}300$$

Simple interest is the convention for short periods within a year, for example money-market deposits (short-term deposits running from a few days to a year) or the supplier credit you will meet in Chapter 3. For multi-year decisions it understates growth, because it ignores that interest which has already been paid out could itself have been reinvested.

### Compound Interest

Under **compound interest** (dt. *Zinseszins*), the interest of each period is added to the balance and earns interest itself in every following period. After one year you have $PV \cdot (1+i)$; after two years $PV \cdot (1+i) \cdot (1+i)$; after $n$ years:

$$FV = PV \cdot (1 + i)^n$$ {#eq-compound}

The factor $(1+i)^n$ is the *compounding factor* (dt. *Aufzinsungsfaktor*). The table shows the mechanics for €1,000 at 10%:

| Year | Opening balance (€) | Interest (€) | Closing balance (€) | Simple interest balance (€) |
|:---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1,000.00 | 100.00 | 1,100.00 | 1,100.00 |
| 2 | 1,100.00 | 110.00 | 1,210.00 | 1,200.00 |
| 3 | 1,210.00 | 121.00 | 1,331.00 | 1,300.00 |

After three years, the gap is only €31, the interest earned on earlier interest. Stretch the horizon to 30 years and the same €1,000 grows to €17,449 under compounding but only €4,000 under simple interest. The difference is not a rounding detail; it is the difference between a straight line and an exponential curve.

The widget below plots both curves for a starting capital of €1,000. Set the rate to 8% and the duration to 30 years: simple interest ends at €3,400, compound interest at about €10,063. Then halve the duration and see how much of the gap disappears. The compound effect is a phenomenon of *long* horizons.

::: {.widget}
<iframe src="assets/ch01/effektzinseszins.html"
        width="100%" height="620px" frameborder="0"
        title="Simple vs. compound interest: growth of 1,000 euros over time for an adjustable interest rate and duration">
</iframe>
:::

A handy mental shortcut is the **Rule of 72**: money roughly doubles after $72 / (\text{interest rate in percent})$ years. At 6% it doubles in about $72 / 6 = 12$ years; the exact answer, derived below, is 11.9 years. At 12% the rule gives 6 years against an exact 6.1 years. The rule is an approximation that works well for rates between about 4% and 12%.

::: {.details}
#### Deep Dive: The Manhattan Myth
In 1626, according to a letter written that year by a Dutch official, the Dutch bought the island of Manhattan from its Lenape inhabitants for goods worth 60 guilders. A 19th-century conversion turned this into the famous figure of "24 dollars". Was it the bargain of the millennium? Suppose the sellers had invested the 24 dollars at 6% compound interest for the 400 years to 2026:

$$FV = 24 \cdot 1.06^{400} \approx 24 \cdot 13{,}254{,}000{,}000 \approx 318{,}000{,}000{,}000$$

About 318 billion dollars, a lot of money, but less than the land of Manhattan is worth today. At 8% instead of 6%, however, the result explodes to roughly 562 *trillion* dollars, more than the entire private wealth of all households on earth today. Two lessons follow. Over long horizons, the result is extremely sensitive to the rate: two percentage points change the answer by a factor of more than 1,700. And the comparison is in nominal dollars across four centuries of inflation, which makes it a better illustration of compounding than an argument about who won the deal.
:::

### Sub-Annual Compounding

Banks often quote an annual rate but credit interest more often: semi-annually, quarterly, monthly. The quoted annual rate $i_{nom}$ is then split into a **relative rate** per sub-period, with $m$ the number of interest periods per year:

$$i_{rel} = \frac{i_{nom}}{m}$$ {#eq-irel}

Interest is compounded with $i_{rel}$ over the total number of sub-periods. For a horizon of $n$ complete years plus $k$ additional sub-periods:

$$FV = PV \cdot (1 + i_{rel})^{n \cdot m + k}$$ {#eq-subannual}

If interest within the horizon is *not* compounded (simple interest, typical for horizons shorter than a year), the same counting applies to the linear formula:

$$FV = PV \cdot \bigl(1 + (n \cdot m + k) \cdot i_{rel}\bigr)$$ {#eq-subannual-simple}

**Example:** €10,000 at a nominal 6% p.a., compounded monthly, for two years and three months. Here $i_{rel} = 0.06 / 12 = 0.005$, $n = 2$, $m = 12$, $k = 3$:

$$FV = 10{,}000 \cdot 1.005^{2 \cdot 12 + 3} = 10{,}000 \cdot 1.005^{27} \approx 11{,}441.52$$

By contrast, €10,000 left in a money-market deposit for four months at 3% simple interest grows to $10{,}000 \cdot (1 + 4 \cdot 0.0025) = 10{,}100$.

More frequent compounding means more interest on interest within the year. To compare offers with different compounding frequencies, convert each one into its **effective annual rate**, the rate that would produce the same result with a single annual compounding:

$$i_{eff} = \left(1 + \frac{i_{nom}}{m}\right)^m - 1$$ {#eq-eff}

For a nominal 6% the table shows what €10,000 becomes after one year:

| Compounding | $m$ | $i_{rel}$ | Value after 1 year (€) | $i_{eff}$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|---:|:---:|
| Annual | 1 | 6.0000% | 10,600.00 | 6.0000% |
| Semi-annual | 2 | 3.0000% | 10,609.00 | 6.0900% |
| Quarterly | 4 | 1.5000% | 10,613.64 | 6.1364% |
| Monthly | 12 | 0.5000% | 10,616.78 | 6.1678% |
| Daily | 365 | 0.0164% | 10,618.31 | 6.1831% |

The effect grows with $m$ but flattens quickly. Even if interest were credited continuously, every instant, the effective rate would only reach $e^{0.06} - 1 \approx 6.1837\%$. The practical lesson: never compare two headline rates with different compounding frequencies; compare their effective rates. In EU consumer lending, this logic is built into the law: lenders must state an annual percentage rate (APR; dt. *effektiver Jahreszins*), which goes one step further and also includes mandatory fees.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Effective Annual Rate
The interest rate that, compounded once a year, produces the same result as a nominal rate compounded $m$ times a year: $i_{eff} = (1 + i_{nom}/m)^m - 1$. It is the only fair basis for comparing offers with different compounding frequencies. For annual compounding ($m = 1$), effective and nominal rate are identical.
:::

::: {.details}
#### Deep Dive: Counting Days
In theory, periods are clean years and months. In practice, banks must decide how to count days, and the convention changes the interest by small but real amounts. Under **30/360** (the German *deutsche Zinsmethode*), every month counts as 30 days and the year as 360. Under **act/360**, the actual number of days is divided by 360; this is the standard for euro money markets such as EURIBOR. Under **act/act (ICMA)**, actual days are divided by the actual days in the period; euro-area government bonds use it. In this course, unless a task says otherwise, periods are complete years or complete months.
:::

### Discounting

Investment decisions almost always need the opposite direction. You pay for a machine *today* and receive its savings *later*. To compare the two, you must bring the future amounts back to $t = 0$. Discounting is compound interest run in reverse. Start from @eq-compound and divide both sides by $(1+i)^n$:

$$PV = \frac{FV}{(1+i)^n} = FV \cdot (1+i)^{-n}$$ {#eq-pv}

The factor $(1+i)^{-n}$ is the **discount factor** (dt. *Abzinsungsfaktor*). For any positive interest rate it is smaller than 1, and it shrinks as $n$ grows. The present value of €10,000 due in two years at 10% is:

$$PV = \frac{10{,}000}{1.10^2} = \frac{10{,}000}{1.21} \approx 8{,}264.46$$

In words: €8,264.46 invested today at 10% grows into exactly €10,000 in two years. The two amounts are *equivalent*; they are the same value seen from two different points on the timeline.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Discount Factor
The factor $(1+i)^{-n}$ that converts a payment due at $t = n$ into its present value at $t = 0$. It is the reciprocal of the compounding factor $(1+i)^n$, always below 1 for a positive rate, and it falls the further away and the higher the rate. Multiply a future payment by it and you have moved that payment to today.
:::

The table shows the discount factors at 8% and what €1,000 received at each point is worth today. Notice that the factors fall by the same proportion every year, not by the same amount.

| $t$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Payment (€) | – | 1,000 | 1,000 | 1,000 | 1,000 | 1,000 |
| Discount factor $1.08^{-t}$ | 1.0000 | 0.9259 | 0.8573 | 0.7938 | 0.7350 | 0.6806 |
| Present value (€) | – | 925.93 | 857.34 | 793.83 | 735.03 | 680.58 |

Together the five payments are worth €3,992.71 today, not €5,000. Chapter 2 shows a shortcut for exactly this kind of sum.

The interactive timeline puts both directions on one axis. Choose a present value, an interest rate and the number of periods: the orange arrow compounds the amount forward to $t = n$, the blue arrow discounts it back. Raise the interest rate and watch the gap between the two ends widen; raise the number of periods and the gap widens even faster.

::: {.widget}
<iframe src="assets/ch01/zeitstrahl.html"
        width="100%" height="560px" frameborder="0"
        title="The Time Machine timeline: compounding moves a value forward, discounting moves it back to t equals 0">
</iframe>
:::

| Direction | Operation | Formula | Effect on value |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| $t = 0 \rightarrow t = n$ | Compounding | $FV = PV \cdot (1+i)^n$ | grows |
| $t = n \rightarrow t = 0$ | Discounting | $PV = FV \cdot (1+i)^{-n}$ | shrinks |

**Worked example: the lottery choice.** You win a prize and may choose between €1,000,000 today (Option A) and €1,100,000 in one year (Option B). The interest rate is 15%. Comparing €1,000,000 with €1,100,000 is meaningless, because the two amounts sit at different points on the timeline. Move B to $t = 0$:

$$PV_B = \frac{1{,}100{,}000}{1.15} \approx 956{,}521.74 < 1{,}000{,}000 = PV_A$$

Option A wins: taking the million today and investing it at 15% would give you €1,150,000 in a year, more than B offers. At an interest rate of 5%, the verdict flips: $PV_B = 1{,}100{,}000 / 1.05 \approx 1{,}047{,}619.05$, and waiting pays. The break-even rate is 10%, the rate at which €1,000,000 grows into exactly €1,100,000. The decision depends not on the size of the payments alone but on the interest rate that links the two points in time.

::: {.drag-exercise}
In the discounting formula, a higher interest rate makes the denominator *larger* and the present value *smaller*, and because the exponent is $n$, this effect hits *distant* payments harder than near ones.
:::

### Real Returns: The Fisher Equation

The Theory section introduced the idea that the real rate is roughly the nominal rate minus inflation. With $\pi$ for the inflation rate and $r$ for the real interest rate, the approximation reads:

$$r \approx i_{nom} - \pi$$ {#eq-fisher-approx}

(In this section only, $r$ denotes the real interest rate; elsewhere in the book it stands for the internal rate of return.) The exact relationship follows from tracking purchasing power. €1 grows to $1 + i_{nom}$ euros in a year, while the price of a basket grows by the factor $1 + \pi$. The number of baskets you can buy therefore grows by:

$$1 + r = \frac{1 + i_{nom}}{1 + \pi} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad r = \frac{1 + i_{nom}}{1 + \pi} - 1$$ {#eq-fisher-exact}

For the euro-area saver from the Theory section (0.5% interest, 10.6% inflation), the approximation gives $0.5\% - 10.6\% = -10.1\%$, the exact formula $1.005 / 1.106 - 1 \approx -9.13\%$. Why the gap? Multiplying out @eq-fisher-exact gives $1 + i_{nom} = (1 + r)(1 + \pi) = 1 + r + \pi + r \cdot \pi$, so $i_{nom} = r + \pi + r \cdot \pi$. The approximation simply drops the product $r \cdot \pi$. For small rates that product is tiny (2% × 3% = 0.06 percentage points), which is why the shortcut works well as long as nominal rate and inflation stay below roughly 10%.

At high inflation the shortcut fails badly. In October 2022, annual consumer price inflation in Turkey reached 85.5%, while the Turkish central bank cut its policy rate to 10.5% in the same month. A saver earning the policy rate would compute:

$$r \approx 10.5\% - 85.5\% = -75.0\% \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad r = \frac{1.105}{1.855} - 1 \approx -40.4\%$$

The loss of purchasing power was brutal in either case, but the approximation overstates it by more than 30 percentage points. When rates are large, use the exact form.

The same logic converts a future nominal amount into today's purchasing power. Deflating by expected inflation over $n$ years is discounting with $\pi$ instead of $i$:

$$\text{Value in today's prices} = \frac{FV}{(1+\pi)^n}$$ {#eq-deflate}

At 2% inflation, €10,000 received in ten years buys what $10{,}000 / 1.02^{10} \approx 8{,}203.48$ euros buy today.

### Solving for the Rate or the Time

@eq-compound links four quantities: $PV$, $FV$, $i$ and $n$. Given any three, you can find the fourth. Solving for the rate gives the annual return that turns $PV$ into $FV$ in $n$ years:

$$i = \left(\frac{FV}{PV}\right)^{1/n} - 1$$ {#eq-solve-i}

Solving for the time uses logarithms:

$$n = \frac{\ln(FV / PV)}{\ln(1+i)}$$ {#eq-solve-n}

**Example:** To grow €200,000 into €280,000 in six years requires $i = (280{,}000 / 200{,}000)^{1/6} - 1 = 1.4^{1/6} - 1 \approx 5.77\%$ per year. And money doubles at 6% after $n = \ln 2 / \ln 1.06 \approx 11.9$ years, the exact value behind the Rule of 72.

### A Five-Step Procedure

Every time-value problem in this book, however dressed up, can be solved with the same five steps:

1. **Draw the timeline.** Mark $t = 0$ and place every payment at its point in time, with inflows and outflows clearly distinguished.
2. **Fix the reference point.** Decide *when* you want to compare the values. For investment decisions this is almost always $t = 0$.
3. **Match rate and period.** Make sure the rate fits the period length: an annual rate for annual periods, $i_{rel}$ for sub-periods, an effective rate when comparing different compounding frequencies, a real rate when the cash flows are in today's prices.
4. **Move every payment** to the reference point: compound with $(1+i)^n$ if it lies to the left, discount with $(1+i)^{-n}$ if it lies to the right.
5. **Compare or add** only values that now sit at the same point in time.

::: {.quick-check}
A supplier offers you €52,000 payable in three years instead of €45,000 today. Your interest rate is 6%. What is the present value of the later payment, and which offer is better for you as the recipient?

- **About €43,660; the €45,000 today is better.**
- About €43,660; the €52,000 is better because it is the larger amount.
- About €61,933; the €52,000 is better.
:::

## Practice: Time Travel in Action

The two cases below apply the five-step procedure. The first returns to Ohtani's contract and shows how much the *reference point* matters; the second is a savings decision in which the highest headline rate turns out to be the worst offer.

### Case Study 1: Ohtani's Deferred Millions

::: {.case-study}
#### Case: The Dodgers' US\$700 Million Contract
The contract signed in December 2023 pays Shohei Ohtani US\$2 million in each playing season from 2024 to 2033 and defers US\$68 million of each season's salary to ten equal, interest-free payments from 2034 to 2043. For simplicity, treat each payment as arriving at the end of its calendar year and take December 2023 as $t = 0$, so the 2024 salary is due at $t = 1$ and the first deferred payment (2034) at $t = 11$.

For its luxury tax, Major League Baseball values deferred salary with the discount rate prescribed by its collective bargaining agreement (the contract between the league and the players' union), 4.43% for this contract, and discounts each deferred US\$68 million back to the season in which it was *earned*, which is ten years before it is paid.

**Tasks:**

1. Compute the annual value the league counts for the luxury tax (salary plus the deferral discounted over ten years), and the total over ten seasons.
2. Compute the present value of the whole contract at signing ($t = 0$) at the same rate of 4.43%.
3. Explain why the two numbers differ and which one tells you what the contract was worth in December 2023.

::: {.solution}
**Solution:**

**1. League (luxury-tax) value.** Each deferral is discounted over ten years, from the season it is earned to the year it is paid. Amounts in millions of US dollars:

$$2 + \frac{68}{1.0443^{10}} = 2 + \frac{68}{1.5426} \approx 2 + 44.08 = 46.08$$

Over ten seasons this gives $10 \times 46.08 \approx 460.8$ million, the "about US\$460 million" that is widely quoted.

**2. Present value at signing.** Step 1, timeline: US\$2 million at $t = 1, \dots, 10$; US\$68 million at $t = 11, \dots, 20$. Step 2, reference point $t = 0$. Steps 3 and 4: discount every payment at 4.43%.

| Year | $t$ | Payment | Discount factor $1.0443^{-t}$ | Present value |
|:---:|:---:|---:|:---:|---:|
| 2024–2033 | 1–10 | 2 each | 0.9576 … 0.6483 | 15.88 (sum) |
| 2034 | 11 | 68 | 0.6208 | 42.21 |
| 2035 | 12 | 68 | 0.5944 | 40.42 |
| 2036 | 13 | 68 | 0.5692 | 38.71 |
| 2037 | 14 | 68 | 0.5451 | 37.06 |
| 2038 | 15 | 68 | 0.5219 | 35.49 |
| 2039 | 16 | 68 | 0.4998 | 33.99 |
| 2040 | 17 | 68 | 0.4786 | 32.54 |
| 2041 | 18 | 68 | 0.4583 | 31.16 |
| 2042 | 19 | 68 | 0.4389 | 29.84 |
| 2043 | 20 | 68 | 0.4202 | 28.58 |
| **Total** | | **700** | | **≈ 365.9** |

Step 5: the deferred payments are worth about US\$350.0 million at signing, the salaries about US\$15.9 million, together roughly **US\$366 million**. At a discount rate of 5% the figure falls further, to about US\$338 million.

**3. Interpretation.** The league's figure answers a different question: it measures each season's pay as of the season itself, so each deferral is discounted over only ten years. The present value at signing moves *every* payment to the same point, December 2023, so the deferred payments are discounted over 11 to 20 years. Only this second number tells you what the contract was worth when it was signed: little more than half its headline value. Ohtani effectively granted the Dodgers a large interest-free loan. The general lesson for the rest of this book: a present value is only meaningful together with its reference point and its discount rate, and two "present values" with different reference points cannot be compared.
:::
:::

### Case Study 2: Three Savings Offers

::: {.case-study}
#### Case: Mia Chooses a Deposit
Mia, a fifth-semester engineering student, has saved €10,000 from her working-student job and wants to lock it away for exactly four years. Three banks compete for her money:

| Offer | Headline rate | Interest terms |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| Bank A | 3.00% p.a. | compounded annually |
| Bank B | 2.98% p.a. | compounded monthly |
| Bank C | 3.10% p.a. | simple interest, paid at maturity |

Mia expects inflation to average 2.0% a year over the four years.

**Tasks:**

1. Compute the effective annual rate of Bank B.
2. Compute the value of Mia's deposit after four years for each offer and rank them.
3. For the best offer, compute the exact real annual return and the value of the final balance in today's prices.

::: {.solution}
**Solution:**

**1. Effective rate of Bank B.** With $i_{rel} = 0.0298 / 12 \approx 0.0024833$ and $m = 12$ (@eq-eff):

$$i_{eff} = \left(1 + \frac{0.0298}{12}\right)^{12} - 1 \approx 3.0210\%$$

**2. Values after four years.**

$$\text{A: } FV = 10{,}000 \cdot 1.03^4 \approx 11{,}255.09$$

$$\text{B: } FV = 10{,}000 \cdot \left(1 + \frac{0.0298}{12}\right)^{4 \cdot 12} = 10{,}000 \cdot 1.0024833^{48} \approx 11{,}264.29$$

$$\text{C: } FV = 10{,}000 \cdot (1 + 4 \cdot 0.031) = 11{,}240.00$$

The ranking by result is **B > A > C**, exactly the reverse of the ranking by headline rate (C > A > B). Bank C's 3.10% looks best but pays no interest on interest; over four years this is equivalent to an effective annual rate of only $1.124^{1/4} - 1 \approx 2.97\%$. Bank B's lower headline rate wins because monthly compounding lifts its effective rate above Bank A's 3.00%. The differences are modest here (€24 between best and worst), but they scale with the amount and the horizon.

**3. Real return of Bank B.** Exact Fisher equation (@eq-fisher-exact):

$$r = \frac{1.030210}{1.020} - 1 \approx 1.00\%$$

In today's prices (@eq-deflate), the final balance is worth:

$$\frac{11{,}264.29}{1.02^4} \approx 10{,}406.46$$

Of Mia's nominal gain of €1,264.29, only about €406 is a real gain in purchasing power; the rest merely compensates for inflation.
:::
:::

::: {.quick-check}
Interest rates rise from 5% to 7%. Which payment loses the larger *share* of its present value: €1,000 due in 2 years or €1,000 due in 20 years?

- Both lose the same share, because the rate rises by the same two percentage points for both.
- The payment due in 2 years, because it is closer to the rate change.
- **The payment due in 20 years: it loses about 31% of its present value, the 2-year payment only about 4%.**
:::

## Conclusion: Time Has a Price

Ohtani's contract is not a curiosity of American sports. It is the purest possible illustration of the idea on which this whole book rests: the size of a payment means nothing until you know *when* it arrives and *which rate* links that moment to today. A euro today is worth more than a euro tomorrow because today's euro can earn interest, because tomorrow's euro may buy less, and because tomorrow's euro may never come. Anyone who accepts less than a euro today in exchange for a euro tomorrow is not being generous. They are simply doing the arithmetic correctly.

From here on, every investment problem will reduce to the same discipline: draw the timeline, fix the reference point, match rate and period, move every payment, then compare. The integrated Hartmann case (Envelope 1) applies exactly these steps to a five-year fixed deposit and its real return, and it is the best way to test yourself before moving on.

::: {.quick-check}
A bank quotes 4.8% p.a., compounded quarterly. What is the effective annual rate?

- 4.80%, because the annual rate is stated as 4.8%.
- **About 4.89%.**
- 1.20%, because a quarter of 4.8% is paid each quarter.
:::

::: {.quick-check}
Your deposit pays a nominal 4% while inflation is 6%. What is the exact real interest rate?

- −2.00%
- **About −1.89%**
- +10.24%
:::

So far we have moved one payment at a time. Chapter 2 turns to the patterns that real contracts produce, whole *streams* of equal payments such as rents, loan instalments and pensions, and shows how to value them in a single step, even a stream that never ends.
